claims.text: Rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 can be obtained in an amorphous state.
The as-quenched alloy has high free volume.
The as-quenched alloy has high internal stresses.
High free volume and internal stresses cause limited amorphous retention in this alloy.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits complex, multistage crystallization during reheating.
A brief anneal slightly below Tg immediately after rapid quenching will reduce excess free volume.
A brief anneal slightly below Tg immediately after rapid quenching will reduce internal residual stresses.
During sub-Tg annealing, atoms can rearrange into a lower-energy amorphous configuration without crystallizing.
Structural relaxation decreases the density of crystallization nucleation sites.
Reduced nucleation-site density and internal stress stabilize the amorphous phase during subsequent thermal cycles.
Post-quench sub-Tg annealing will improve amorphous retention over a broader range of cooling rates than in untreated material.
Post-quench sub-Tg annealing will increase the onset temperature of crystallization during reheating.
Post-quench sub-Tg annealing may produce a simpler and more stable thermal response during reheating.
The initial cooling rate must be sufficient to bypass crystallization before the annealing treatment is applied.
Annealing too close to or above the crystallization regime, or for too long, may initiate crystallization and negate the benefit.
The optimal annealing temperature and duration depend on the alloy's Tg and relaxation kinetics.
DSC can compare crystallization onset and peak profiles between annealed and untreated samples.
XRD and TEM can compare amorphous and crystalline phase content between annealed and untreated samples.

contradictions.description: The intervention occurs only after rapid quenching, so it cannot improve glass formation or amorphous retention during the already-completed solidification step or enable slower prior cooling rates. It can only affect post-quench stability and reheating behavior.
